checks: An interior point of a limiting fiber lies in a positive centered ball in that fiber, so uniform support convergence implies eventual inclusion. Exterior points are eventually excluded, and the convex-body boundary is Lebesgue null. Bounded convergence on the common ball yields symmetric-difference convergence and convergence of raw moments through order two. Positive limiting masses allow division in the centroid and covariance formulas.

Each nonzero direction has positive within-fiber variance because its level hyperplanes have zero volume in a full-dimensional fiber. Uniform quadratic-form convergence on the unit sphere and uniform continuity of the square root yield uniform convergence of the induced norm. The covariance here has no between-fiber centroid term.

For any violating energy pairs, finiteness of P and compactness give a fixed base and a common limiting mark since ‖y_j−y‖≤δ_j→0. The predecessor applies both to the moving family and the constant limiting body, even when the common mark is on the boundary. Each j-mark has a counterpart, so the multiplier hypothesis and compactness of the limiting lifted union give a uniform bound on the multipliers. Energy and mass bounds then place the root arguments in a common compact interval including zero, where the root is uniformly continuous. The convergent ε_j and covariance norms give the asserted Δ_j→0.

For u≠0, divide a and u by ‖u‖, using positive homogeneity of the covariance norm. The threshold at measured base z is u·y−a·(z−p) minus the buffer for this normalized pair. Both comparisons keep p,z,a,u fixed, so the entire base term cancels without a bound on a. At a fixed threshold the cap mass change is at most V_j, and the remaining strip change is at most LΔ_j by slicing the limiting fibers. This includes supporting and saturated closed cuts. In d=1 the strip volume is at most its interval length per fiber.

For u=0, the tested nonzero a selects exactly the same bases in both families, including every base on the equality plane. The mass change is at most V_j. When n=0 this class of directions is absent and the nonzero continuous normals still give a nonempty comparison set. The uniform per-cap inequality yields the two-sided infimum inequality without assuming attainment in the direction variable.

At any fixed j the predecessor with a constant body gives continuity of the energy and thus of f_j on each fiber. The same within-family strip comparison gives uniform-in-normal continuity in the mark, so the infimum is continuous. Compactness gives attainment in the mark variable. Counterparts exist in both directions at the same base by Hausdorff distance; applying the uniform comparison at a maximizing mark on either side proves convergence of maxima, and M_j→M_0>0 gives the normalized claim.

A pure-base cap through such an outside base can miss P entirely and has mass zero, so allowing such marks cannot raise the mixed maximum.
